introduction.definition: A dense-phase pneumatic system conveys alumina in batches. A blow tank is filled through a dome valve, sealed, pressurised and the alumina is pushed through the pipeline as slow-moving plugs. Low velocity limits attrition and pipe wear.

pressure.title: Low velocity, high pressure: gentle on alumina
pressure.description: In dense phase the blow tank is pressurised (often ~ 2–6 bar) and the alumina moves as slow plugs or dunes (typically ~ 2–10 m/s) rather than suspended at high speed. This greatly reduces particle breakage (attrition creates fines/dust that smelters dislike) and pipe wear, and needs less air than dilute-phase conveying.

video_tutorials.title: Alumina Pneumatic Conveying System — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Alumina Pneumatic Conveying System.
A dense-phase pneumatic system conveys alumina in batches.
A blow tank is filled through a dome valve, sealed, pressurised and the alumina is pushed through the pipeline as slow-moving plugs.
Low velocity limits attrition and pipe wear.
Typical applications include alumina transfer to silos and smelter pot-feeding systems; conveying abrasive or friable powders (cement, fly ash, catalysts).
The cutaway reveals the internal construction.
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.
Next, watch the operation tutorial to see how it works.

script.narration: How the Alumina Pneumatic Conveying System works.
The dome valve opens and the blow tank fills.
The tank is sealed and pressurised.
Plugs move through the line.
The receiving silo collects the alumina.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.
In dense phase the blow tank is pressurised (often ~ 2–6 bar) and the alumina moves as slow plugs or dunes (typically ~ 2–10 m/s) rather than suspended at high speed.

video_tutorials.title: Alumina Pneumatic Conveying System — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Alumina Pneumatic Conveying System.
Check cycle times and pressures.
Inspect dome valve seal.
Replace bends.
Watch for line blockage: pressure rises, no flow. Common cause: wet product, booster fault.
Watch for seal leakage: long cycles. Common cause: worn dome seal.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
